02.event: Rabbi Akiva, who used to ridicule transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman at the top of a palm tree and began climbing it.
02.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him and said that only the heavenly proclamation protecting Rabbi Akiva and his Torah saved him from ruin.
02.outcome: Rabbi Akiva was spared, shown that he was not immune to temptation.
02.summary: Rabbi Akiva used to mock people who sinned. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he grabbed the trunk and began to climb. Halfway up, Satan dropped the disguise and told him he would have been destroyed were it not for a heavenly announcement to take care of Rabbi Akiva and his Torah.

03.actor: A half-maidservant, half-free woman and her master
03.event: The court forced the master of a half-maidservant to free her entirely.
03.turn: The master was compelled to emancipate her.
03.summary: Rav Huna bar Ketina reports in Rabbi Yitzhak's name an incident of a woman who was half slave and half free. The court forced her master to free her, and he made her a free woman. Only this bare result is given; the reason is argued over afterwards.
03.missing: Who the people were, why the master was forced, and any scene; the passage only reports the outcome as a precedent.

04.actor: A creditor and the herdsman of orphans' cattle, before Rav Nahman
04.event: A creditor seized an ox of orphans, claiming he took it while the debtor was alive, while the herdsman said it was after death, and they came before Rav Nahman.
04.turn: Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses and he had none.
04.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that since the creditor could claim he bought it, he could equally claim he seized it during the debtor's lifetime, so the creditor's claim stood.
04.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans' cattle. He said he seized it before the debtor died, and the herdsman said it was after. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses, and he had none, so Rav Nahman reasoned the creditor's claim must be accepted.

05.event: Mar Shmuel permitted his household to place a large mortar against the door to secure it.
05.turn: He judged that the mortar counted as a utensil, so using it was not building.
05.outcome: The mortar was allowed to be used as a door bolt.
05.summary: In Mar Shmuel's house there was a large mortar. He allowed it to be set against the door to secure it, saying it had the status of a utensil.
05.missing: This is a brief precedent case with a ruling rather than a story with a real turn or ending.

06.event: Mar Ukva sent a pauper in his neighborhood 400 dinars every year on the eve of Yom Kippur, and one year sent them with his son.
06.turn: The son came back saying the man did not need it because he saw them pouring old wine for him.
06.outcome: Mar Ukva reasoned that a man so pampered needed more, and doubled the sum.
06.summary: Mar Ukva yearly sent a poor neighbor 400 dinars before Yom Kippur. One year his son brought it and returned saying the man didn't need help, since old wine was being sprinkled for him. Mar Ukva concluded that someone used to such luxury needed even more, so he doubled the gift and sent it.

07.event: Funerals had become so costly that relatives abandoned the dead and fled, until Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in plain linen.
07.turn: Rabban Gamliel set a modest example.
07.outcome: All the people followed, and even now plain burial garments are customary.
07.summary: Funerals once cost relatives more than the death itself, to the point that they left the body and fled. Rabban Gamliel then arranged to be taken out for burial in plain linen, and everyone followed his example. Rav Pappa notes that people today bury even in cheap cloth.
07.missing: A specific scene; it is a short account of a change in custom, not a single dramatized event.

08.event: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphan nephew, Ravina the younger, and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
08.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the orphan's wine along.
08.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine was no better than his own.
08.summary: Ravina was looking after wine belonging to his orphaned nephew and also had his own wine to carry to Sikhra to sell. He asked Rav Ashi if he could take the orphan's wine too, and Rav Ashi told him to go ahead, since the orphan's was no better than his own.

09.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
09.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
09.turn: Wheat then arrived, making the sales unnecessary.
09.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions be returned to their owners.
09.summary: In a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat. Then wheat arrived and the sales proved unnecessary. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions go back to their former owners.

10.event: A very beautiful woman, besieged by men wanting to betroth her, claimed to be already betrothed.
10.turn: Later she betrothed herself to a man, and the Sages asked why.
10.outcome: She explained she had said it to fend off unworthy suitors, and the Sages at Usha ruled that a statement with a rationale is believed.
10.summary: A beautiful woman was pursued by many men and told them she was already betrothed. Later she betrothed herself to someone, and the Sages asked why. She said the earlier men were unworthy and the later one was worthy, and the Sages ruled she is believed since she gave a reason.

11.actor: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya and Rav
11.event: Rav Hinnana taught a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav before Rav in a wording that matched Rabbi Meir's stringent view.
11.turn: Rav rebuked him for abandoning the Rabbis and following Rabbi Meir.
11.outcome: The Gemara explains Rav Hinnana's reasoning and says the first clause follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Meir.
11.summary: Rav Hinnana was teaching a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in Rav's presence and gave a wording matching Rabbi Meir. Rav asked him whether he had abandoned the Rabbis to follow Rabbi Meir.
11.missing: Little event beyond a corrected teaching; the rest is legal explanation.

12.event: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat so immersed himself in Torah that he studied in Tzippori's lower marketplace while his cloak lay in the upper marketplace.
12.turn: One time someone came to take the cloak.
12.outcome: He found a serpent on it guarding it.
12.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah that he sat studying in one marketplace of Tzippori and left his cloak lying in another. Once a person came to take it and found a serpent on it.

13.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch, and Rav Yosef
13.event: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace, and Rav Aha bar Huna sent the question of what to do to Rav Yosef.
13.turn: The case was unclear since a myrtle branch might or might not be worth a peruta.
13.outcome: Rav Yosef replied to flog the man, as Rav would, and require a bill of divorce, as Shmuel would.
13.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace. Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef, who replied to flog the man in line with Rav and also require a get in line with Shmuel, in case the branch was worth a peruta somewhere.

14.event: The Sages, faced with Shmuel's and Karna's conflicting statements, noted that Mar Ukva's court was nearby and also sent the question to Rav with the opinions' names reversed.
14.turn: Rav swore that she needs both a get and refusal, and denied Shmuel would say otherwise.
14.outcome: Rav ruled that she needs both.
14.summary: When Karna challenged Shmuel's ruling as self-contradictory, the Sages suggested asking Mar Ukva's court nearby. They also switched the names and sent the question to Rav. Rav swore that she needs both a get and refusal and that Shmuel could not have said otherwise.
14.missing: Who spoke to whom and the full setup of the test are only hinted at.

15.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
15.event: She brought the orphans to court to claim her marriage contract.
15.turn: The orphans said it was demeaning for her to appear in house clothes, so she dressed in all her clothes.
15.outcome: Ravina ruled that the court appraises what a widow is wearing, so her clothes were counted against her marriage contract.
15.summary: A widow was taking the orphans of her husband's house to court for her marriage contract. They told her it was shameful to go in plain clothes, so she put on all her clothes. Before Ravina, he ruled that the court appraises what a widow wears, so everything she had on was counted.

16.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave, a gentile woman, Rav Yosef
16.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman for the sake of intimate relations.
16.turn: Rav Yosef said he could render her and her daughter fit to marry into Israel.
16.outcome: Rav Yosef's ruling is stated; its reasoning follows in the next segments.
16.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman for the sake of intimacy. Rav Yosef said he could treat both her and her daughter as fit to marry into the community.
16.missing: The result is a ruling, and the reasons are in later segments; there is little narrative.

17.actor: A man suffering from love for a woman
17.event: A man in Eretz Yisrael was tormented over a certain woman and wanted to leave the land.
17.turn: He heard the teaching about the great significance of living in Eretz Yisrael.
17.outcome: He stayed in the land and suffered until his death.
17.summary: Ilfa told of a man in Eretz Yisrael who suffered over a woman and sought to leave. When he heard the teaching about the merit of living in Eretz Yisrael, he stayed and endured it until he died.
17.missing: The man is not named, and the story sits inside a letter to Rabba that is mostly advice.

18.actor: A man claiming to be from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
18.event: A man said he was from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood and said Shot Mishot lies between the rivers.
18.outcome: The rest is discussion of why it matters and where the boundaries are.
18.summary: A man told the Sages he came from Shot Mishot. Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood and pointed out that the place lies between the rivers, which bears on questions of lineage.
18.missing: What happened to the man and the point of the remark; the passage turns into a boundary discussion.

19.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish while having a case before him, and Rav Anan said he was disqualified from judging his case.
19.turn: The man explained the gift as a first-fruits-style offering to a scholar, so Rav Anan accepted it, then sent the man to Rav Nahman with a letter saying he was disqualified.
19.outcome: Rav Nahman, assuming the man was Rav Anan's relative, put aside an orphans' case to honor him, and the other litigant, seeing this, was cowed and lost.
19.summary: A man with a lawsuit brought Rav Anan a basket of fish, and Rav Anan refused it and said he could not judge the case. The man said he wanted only to give the gift, citing the first-fruits teaching, and Rav Anan accepted, then sent him to Rav Nahman with a note that he was disqualified. Rav Nahman assumed the man was a relative, set aside an orphans' case to judge his, and the opponent was so cowed by the honor shown that he lost.

20.event: A woman wanted to say to her friend 'come and I will feed you milk'.
20.turn: Her imprecise speech made it come out as 'may a lioness eat you'.
20.outcome: She said the wrong thing, showing the imprecision of Galilean speech.
20.summary: A Galilean woman meant to invite her neighbor over for milk. Because of her imprecise pronunciation, what she actually said was 'may a lioness eat you'.
